title: Factors, multiples and primes
summary: Arrange counters into rectangles to find a number's factors. See why some numbers make only one rectangle.
guide: This studio covers Year 4–6 work on factors, multiples and primes. The number of counters stays the same and only the row length changes. If the row length is not a {{term:factor}} of the number, the last row is short.

Each rectangle is a factor pair: 12 = 3 × 4 means 3 and 4 are factors of 12, and 12 is a {{term:multiple}} of 3 and of 4. A number with exactly two factors (1 and itself) is a {{term:prime-number}}; the others are composite. 1 is neither prime nor composite.

In the last mission a factor tree breaks a number down until every branch ends in a prime ({{term:prime-factorisation}}). Common slips: forgetting 1 and the number itself, counting pairs instead of factors, and thinking every odd number (like 9) is prime.

engine.instruction-tap: Use − and + to change the row length.
engine.instruction-tree: Tap a number to split it into two factors.

rectangles-of-twelve.title: Rectangles of 12
rectangles-of-twelve.prompt: You have 12 counters. Arrange them in 3 equal rows. How many counters are in each row?
rectangles-of-twelve.hint: Use + to make the rows longer until there are just 3 full rows and no short row.
rectangles-of-twelve.success: Well done! 12 = 3 × 4. So 3 and 4 are factors of 12, and 12 is a multiple of 3 and of 4.
rectangles-of-twelve.why: Make the rows 5 long. Why is 5 not a factor of 12?
rectangles-of-twelve.model: Rows of 5 give two full rows (10 counters) and a short row of 2. 12 can't be split into equal rows of 5; 12 ÷ 5 leaves a remainder of 2. So 5 is not a factor of 12.

feedback.not-rect: The last row is short. Change the row length so every row is full.
feedback.wrong-array: You need exactly 3 full rows. Count the rows.
feedback.subtracted: You worked out 12 − 3. We arranged 12 in 3 equal rows; count one row.
feedback.rows: 3 is the number of rows. Count the counters in one row.
feedback.too-big: Count the counters in one row again.
feedback.too-small: Count the counters in one row again.
feedback.empty: Now tap the number for your answer.

factors-of-eighteen.title: All the factors of 18
factors-of-eighteen.prompt: You have 18 counters. Try every row length from 1 to 18. Each length that makes a full rectangle is a factor of 18. How many factors does 18 have?
factors-of-eighteen.hint: Try the lengths in order: 1, 2, 3, … and note each one that leaves no short row. Don't forget 1 and 18.
factors-of-eighteen.success: Well done! The factors of 18 are 1, 2, 3, 6, 9 and 18: six factors in three pairs, 1 × 18, 2 × 9 and 3 × 6.
factors-of-eighteen.why: Once you reach 3 × 6, why don't you need to try the longer rows?
factors-of-eighteen.model: Factors come in pairs. After 3 × 6 the pairs repeat the other way round: 6 × 3, 9 × 2, 18 × 1. Each bigger factor was already found with its smaller partner.

feedback.not-rect: The last row is short. Make a full rectangle.
feedback.pairs: 3 is the number of pairs (1 × 18, 2 × 9, 3 × 6). Each pair has two factors.
feedback.forgot-ends: Don't forget 1 and 18 itself. 18 counters in 1 row is a rectangle too.
feedback.the-number: 18 is the number itself. Count its factors.
feedback.missed-one: You missed one. Try the lengths 1 to 9 again.
feedback.too-big: Some lengths leave a short row; those are not factors.
feedback.too-small: There are more factors. Count 1 and 18 as well.
feedback.empty: Now tap the number for your answer.

prime-thirteen.title: A number with one rectangle
prime-thirteen.prompt: You have 13 counters. Try every row length. How many factors does 13 have?
prime-thirteen.hint: Try 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6. Does any of them make a full rectangle?
prime-thirteen.success: Well done! 13 has only two factors: 1 and 13. So 13 is a prime number.
prime-thirteen.model: No. A prime has exactly two different factors: 1 and itself. 1 has only one factor (itself), so it is not prime, and it is not composite either.

feedback.not-rect: The last row is short. Make a full rectangle (even a single row of 13).
feedback.only-one: 1 is a factor of 13. But 13 is also a factor of itself.
feedback.the-number: 13 is the number itself. Count its factors.
feedback.not-a-factor: Did you find a length that leaves no short row? Try again: none from 2 to 12 works.
feedback.too-big: Only lengths that make a full rectangle are factors.
feedback.empty: Now tap the number for your answer.

tree-of-sixty.title: A factor tree for 60
tree-of-sixty.prompt: Tap 60 and split it into two factors. Keep splitting every number that isn't prime until every branch ends in a prime. Then find the missing number.
tree-of-sixty.hint: Primes turn green and can't be split. If a number is still a button, it isn't prime.
tree-of-sixty.success: Well done! 60 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 5. This is the {{term:prime-factorisation}} of 60.
tree-of-sixty.why: Ali starts with 60 = 6 × 10 and Sara with 60 = 4 × 15. Do they end with the same primes? Why?
tree-of-sixty.model: Yes. Ali: 6 = 2 × 3 and 10 = 2 × 5. Sara: 4 = 2 × 2 and 15 = 3 × 5. Both reach 2, 2, 3, 5. Every composite number is a product of primes in only one way; the order of splitting doesn't matter.

feedback.tree-unfinished: There's still a branch that isn't prime. Tap it and split it.
feedback.not-prime: That number isn't prime; it can still be split. We want primes only.
feedback.too-big: Look at the ends of the branches.
feedback.too-small: Look at the ends of the branches.
feedback.empty: Now tap the number for your answer.
